section_summary: This section comprises the concluding pages and associated enclosures of an extensive U.S. Embassy Tokyo diplomatic report on second-generation Japanese (Nisei) residing in Japan. It presents statistical analyses of Nisei immigration, expatriation, and demographics, alongside assessments of Japanese official policy and the social attitudes of resident Americans. It also includes questionnaires and survey tabulations by the Tokyo YMCA, a roster of the Japan Cultural Forum, course catalogues for the School of Japanese Language and Culture and the Waseda International Institute, a prospectus for the Kaigai Kyoiku Kyokai preparatory school, and newspaper articles from The Japan Times & Mail and The Japan Advertiser on Nisei social and theatrical activities.

subfiles.about: Concluding portion of a comprehensive diplomatic report analyzing expatriation, immigration statistics, demographics, and social conditions of second-generation Japanese residing in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Discusses the expatriation of second-generation Japanese renouncing Japanese nationality under revised nationality laws, noting that over ninety-nine percent of those renouncing nationality were American or Hawaiian Nisei. Evaluates migration and census statistics compiled by Professor Edward K. Strong, Jr. alongside port records from Seattle, San Francisco, Los Angeles, and Honolulu, estimating that approximately 40,000 second-generation Japanese lived in Japan in 1930, of whom about 1,000 were American-educated temporary residents (Group C). Concludes on page 42 with drafter initials RFB/rk, followed on page 43 by an itemized list of enclosures filed with the report.
subfiles.title: Report on Second-Generation Japanese in Japan (Pages 31-43 and List of Enclosures)

subfiles.about: Diplomatic memorandum evaluating the Japanese Government's cultural diplomacy and financial assistance directed toward second-generation Japanese students.
subfiles.summary: Enclosure 1(a): Japan's Foreign Office seeks goodwill among Nisei students as informal cultural ambassadors, funding groups like the Kaigai Kyoiku Kyokai; Japan's cultural expansion should be recognized and monitored.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 1.(a): The Japanese Government [Government Aid to Second-Generation Japanese]

subfiles.about: Brief diplomatic memorandum analyzing the limited interest and social aloofness exhibited by resident Americans in Japan toward second-generation Japanese.
subfiles.summary: Enclosure 1(b): American colonies, mission schools and clubs in Japan take almost no interest in Nisei, with a few educators at Waseda and the YMCA; long-term business residents would oppose admitting Nisei to American clubs.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 1.(b): Assistance from Americans in Japan

subfiles.about: Newspaper review of an English-language stage production of Kikuchi Kan's play Katakiuchi Ijyo performed by the Pacific Young People's Society in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Japan Times & Mail review of Glenn Shaw's English translation of Kikuchi Kan's "Better Than Revenge" by Nisei youth of the Pacific Young People's Society, praising Satoru Sugimura and Himeko Nishikawa; proceeds fund cultural research trips.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 3.(c): "Famous Play by Kikuchi Kan Given in English" (The Japan Times & Mail)

subfiles.about: Blank questionnaire distributed by the Tokyo YMCA to survey the personal background, education, and social adjustment of second-generation Japanese in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Five-section questionnaire for Nisei in the U.S. and Japan on birthplaces, family, education, reasons for coming to Japan, job difficulties, advantages, loneliness, prejudice, and plans to stay or return.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 4.(a): Copy of Questionnaire

subfiles.about: Statistical report tabulating and analyzing responses from 104 questionnaires collected during a census of second-generation Japanese conducted by the Tokyo YMCA.
subfiles.summary: YMCA 1934-1935 Nisei census of 104 respondents, 66 men and 38 women: birthplaces mostly California and Hawaii, enrollment at Meiji, Waseda and Nihon, careers, job obstacles, and what they like in Japan against frustrations over police, living standards and loneliness.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 4.(b): Results Taken from the Second Generation Census Taken by the Y.M.C.A. 1934-1935

subfiles.about: Membership roster of the Japan Cultural Forum in Tokyo detailing the educational background and employment of seventeen prominent American-educated Nisei.
subfiles.summary: Roster of seventeen Japan Cultural Forum members with American colleges and Tokyo and Yokohama jobs, including Goro Murata, George Togasaki and RIKEN researchers.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 5: The Japan Cultural Forum Members

subfiles.about: Official course catalogue and bulletin of the School of Japanese Language and Culture and the School for Foreign-Born Japanese at the Tokyo City YMCA for 1935-1936.
subfiles.from: School of Japanese Language and Culture (City Y.M.C.A., Tokyo)
keywords: School of Japanese Language and Culture
subfiles.summary: Sets forth the academic calendar, trustees, faculty, and curricula for the School of Japanese Language and Culture (established in 1913 under Director Frank Muller) and its branch School for Foreign-Born Japanese. Outlines three-year direct-method language courses, specialized courses for religious workers, correspondence extension classes, and cultural lectures in Japanese history, art, government, and family systems. Details admission requirements, tuition schedules, dormitories, and student counseling services directed by Executive Secretary Kazuya Matsumiya and Director Darley Downs.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 2.(a): Bulletin of the School of Japanese Language and Culture (Nichigo Bunka Gakkō)

subfiles.about: Bilingual prospectus and institutional regulations for the preparatory school founded at Waseda Hoshien to prepare overseas Japanese students for Waseda University.
subfiles.summary: Presents the regulations, curriculum, faculty, and background of the Waseda International Institute, organized under President Tadaoki Yamamoto and Dr. H. B. Benninghoff to prepare overseas Japanese students for entrance into Waseda University. The English text (pages 206-217) outlines preparatory curricula in Japanese language, Chinese, English, mathematics, and culture, while summarizing Waseda Hoshien's Christian student ministry at Scott Hall and Waseda University's academic departments. The Japanese text (pages 218-235) contains formal school bylaws, living cost guidelines, and an inspiring call for Nisei to master both cultures and serve as leaders in international relations.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 2.(b): Waseda International Institute [Prospectus and Regulations]

subfiles.about: Illustrated Japanese prospectus and admission guide for the boarding facilities and preparatory tutorial school operated by the Kaigai Kyoiku Kyokai at Masugatayama.
subfiles.from: Kaigai Kyoiku Kyokai (Institute for the Education of Overseas Japanese)
subfiles.summary: Prospectus of the Kaigai Kyoiku Kyokai's preparatory school and dormitories under Viscount Kikujiro Ishii, at Masugatayama in Kanagawa, with photographs, advisors Saito, Hirota, Kodama and Okada, fees, and university entrance help.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 2.(c): Kaigai Kyoiku Kyokai Dormitory and Preparatory School Prospectus [寄宿寮・補導學校 入寮入學案内]

subfiles.about: Newspaper article discussing the cultural responsibilities and historical background of second-generation Japanese youth following an America-Japan Society sociable.
subfiles.summary: Japan Advertiser: T. H. Shimanouchi covers the America-Japan Society's Lincoln's Birthday reception at Mitsukoshi for 400 Nisei and 200 members, on Nisei as a "bridge of peace," their Issei parents' hardships before the 1924 exclusion act, and needed support; continues.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 3.(a): "Second Generation Cast in Hard Role" (The Japan Advertiser)
